newsitem.title: USA: Dow ends lower as investors turn to smaller stocks.
newsitem.headline: Dow ends lower as investors turn to smaller stocks.

text.p: Stocks ended mixed Monday as the shares of some overlooked smaller companies rose at the expense of larger blue-chip issues.

The Dow Jones industrial average fell 41.64 points to 7,289.40. Beyond the blue-chip market, however, gainers outpaced losers by 1,534 to 968 on volume of 432.6 million on the New York Stock Exchange.
"We're continuing to see some rotation out of big stocks and into small stocks," said Alan Ackerman, market strategist at Fahnestock & Co.
"The Dow has made a strong move over the last couple of weeks and it looks like some people are cashing in now," Ackerman said. "There are a lot of economic numbers ahead."

Other broader market measures also rose. The Russell 2000 index of smaller stocks added 2.76 points to 383.52, the American Stock Exchange index, also weighted towards smaller stocks, edged up 1.79 to 607.17, and the Nasdaq index added 4.47 to 1,404.79.
Analysts said a slew of economic data -- including the monthly employment report due on Friday -- probably would put a damper on demand for blue-chip stocks the next few days.

Even after Monday's decline, the Dow stands nearly 900 points higher than it did on April 11. In contrast, smaller stocks have only recently begun to shake off a malaise that had extended for more than a year.
If investors were cautious to start the week, that concern intensified with release of the week's first important economic indicator, the National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) index.

The index, a gauge of manufacturing activity compiled by purchasers at about 300 major corporations, rose to 57.1 in May, soundly beating economists' forecasts for a 53.9 reading, as well as April's level of 54.2. A reading above 50 percent signals the manufacturing sector is growing while one below that level points to contraction.

Analysts said some of the strength appeared to be linked to special factors, such as the end of a strike at a Chrysler Corp. motor plant. But even after such factors, analysts said the index hinted that the upcoming jobs report would be a strong one.
"Employment really drives that (NAPM) number a lot," said Robert Froehlich, chief investment strategist at Kemper Funds. "Manufacturing can only be strong if employment is strong."

Froehlich said the bond market's muted response to the report may have been because of strong global demand for U.S. assets, particularly from Europe, where currency issues and political uncertainties have mounted.

"It's going to be months before we figure out the impact of the elections in France and Great Britain," he said. "In the interim, a lot of foreign money is coming into this market as a hiding place, so to speak."
The bond market largely shrugged off the report, and the benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury climbed 3/32, reducing the yield to 6.90 percent from 6.91 percent at Friday's close.
Among Dow components, Procter & Gamble Co. fell 4-1/4 to 133-5/8 after Smith Barney downgraded the shares to outperform from buy.

Elsewhere, PepsiCo rose one to 37-3/4 after the company said it would reorganize its North American beverage business, creating a separate unit for its bottling operations. Pepsi denied suggestions from Wall Street analysts that the move was intended to prepare for a spinoff of its bottling operations.

G&K Services Inc. fell two to 30-3/4 after the company said it would acquire the uniform rental business of National Linen Service for about $287 million. National Service Industries, parent of National Linen, slipped 5/8 to 43-1/4.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks fell 1.92 to 846.36.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 0.24 to 441.54. The average price per share fell 2 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 8,044.456, up 5.957 or 0.07 percent.
